prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current approaches for Radar-Camera depth estimation struggle to balance efficiency with accuracy due to the inherent sparsity and noise of mmWave Radar data. The prevailing paradigm relies on complex, multi-stage frameworks that first attempt to generate an intermediate "quasi-dense" depth map to bridge the gap between sparse radar returns and dense image pixels. This intermediate step creates a significant bottleneck: it is computationally expensive, preventing real-time performance, and often introduces noise or artifacts when the intermediate prediction fails (e.g., in adverse lighting). We identify the reliance on this intermediate, unstable representation as the primary obstacle to robust and efficient sensor fusion.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that accurate dense depth can be predicted in a **single stage**, without generating intermediate quasi-dense representations, by fundamentally rethinking how Radar information is extracted and fused.

Our hypothesis is twofold:
1.  **Structural Integrity:** Treating Radar points as a graph rather than isolated measurements will allow us to capture geometric topology, making the system more robust to noise and outliers.
2.  **Implicit Correspondence:** We can bypass explicit depth densification by learning cross-modal correlations directly through a hierarchical fusion mechanism that aligns image features with Radar structures based on spatial proximity.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to design a streamlined, one-stage framework consisting of two primary conceptual modules:

**1. Graph-Based Radar Structure Extractor**
Instead of processing Radar points as independent coordinates, we will represent the point cloud as a graph.
*   **Node & Edge Representation:** We will treat individual Radar returns as nodes and their spatial relationships as edges.
*   **Feature Extraction:** By applying Graph Neural Network (GNN) principles, we will aggregate information across neighbors. This allows the model to learn the local geometry and topology of the scene, providing a feature set that is far more robust to individual noisy points than simple coordinate-based extraction.

**2. Pyramid-Based Radar Fusion with Spatially-Constrained Attention**
We plan to integrate the extracted Radar graphs with image features using a hierarchical (pyramid) approach.
*   **Hierarchical Levels:**
    *   **Shallow Layers:** We will fuse fine-grained image details with raw Radar coordinates to capture low-level spatial cues.
    *   **Deep Layers:** We will fuse high-level scene semantics with the extracted Radar graph structures.
*   **Radar-Centered Flash Attention:** To solve the efficiency problem of associating sparse points with dense pixels, we will implement a specialized cross-modal attention mechanism.
    *   *Intuition:* Since Radar horizontal resolution is generally reliable while elevation is ambiguous, we will restrict the attention calculation for each Radar point to a specific horizontal window of image pixels.
    *   *Benefit:* This "masked" attention avoids global computation, drastically reducing overhead while implicitly learning the correspondence between the visual data and the depth measurements.

**3. Flexible Inference Architecture**
We propose to design the input layer to be adaptable. The model will include an auxiliary branch capable of ingesting an optional initial relative depth map. This will allow the model to function in two modes:
*   **Independent:** Consuming only raw sensor data for maximum speed.
*   **Plug-in:** Acting as a metric scale refiner for external relative depth estimators when higher accuracy is required.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical:** We aim to demonstrate that intermediate quasi-dense representations are unnecessary for sparse-to-dense fusion, effectively simplifying the standard pipeline for this task.
*   **Methodological:** The introduction of a graph-based structure extractor for Radar depth tasks offers a new way to handle sensor sparsity and noise compared to traditional coordinate-mapping techniques.
*   **Practical:** By moving to a one-stage architecture with optimized attention mechanisms, we expect to achieve a significant reduction in inference latency, enabling real-time deployment on autonomous systems without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed a comprehensive experimental framework to evaluate "TacoDepth," a one-stage Radar-Camera fusion network for depth estimation. The experiments focused on assessing depth accuracy, model efficiency (inference speed, parameters, FLOPs), and flexibility between independent and plug-in inference modes.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **nuScenes:** Outdoor driving dataset with cameras, 3D Radar, and LiDAR. We used the standard split: 700 scenes for training, 150 for validation, and 150 for testing. The dataset contains approximately 40,000 synchronized keyframes. Ground truth depth ($D_{gt}$) was generated by accumulating LiDAR points from 160 nearby frames. Input image resolution: $900 \times 1600$.
    *   **ZJU-4DRadarCam:** Collected with a ground robot using cameras, 4D Radar, and LiDAR. This dataset provides denser Radar data. We used the official split: 29,312 frames for training/validation and 4,097 frames for testing. Ground truth was obtained via linear interpolation of LiDAR depth. Input image resolution: $300 \times 1280$.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Depth Accuracy:** Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Inverse MAE (iMAE), Inverse RMSE (iRMSE), Relative Error (Rel), and $\delta_1$ (accuracy within threshold).
    *   **Evaluation Ranges:** We evaluated at maximum distances of 0-50m, 0-70m, and 0-80m.
    *   **Efficiency:** Inference time (ms), Frames Per Second (fps), Parameters (M), and Floating Point Operations (FLOPs).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Independent Models:** Lin et al., RC-PDA, R4Dyn, DORN, Singh et al., CaFNet, Li et al.
    *   **Plug-in Models:** RadarCam-Depth.
    *   **Relative Depth Predictors (for Plug-in mode):** DPT-Hybrid, MiDaS-v3.1, Depth-Anything-v2.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Training was conducted on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Efficiency metrics were measured on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (for nuScenes comparison) or NVIDIA A6000 (for efficiency analysis).
    *   **Model Architecture:** Image encoder utilized ResNet-18. The graph-based Radar structure extractor used $L=3$ GNN layers. The widths of Radar-centered flash attention areas ($a_l$) were set to $\{48, 32, 16\}$ for the three layers.
    *   **Training Configuration:**
        *   **Optimizer:** Adam.
        *   **Batch Size:** 12.
        *   **Epochs:** 50.
        *   **Learning Rate:** Initial rate of $1e^{-4}$, decaying by $1e^{-5}$ every 10 epochs.
        *   **Loss Function:** L1 loss with coefficient $\lambda = 1$.
        *   **Strategy:** Data was randomly divided; half used the auxiliary branch with initial relative depth (plug-in mode training), and the other half used zero input (independent mode training).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Efficiency and Accuracy Trade-offs (from Figure 1 Analysis):**
*   We observed that TacoDepth (Independent) achieves significantly lower inference time (smaller circle size) compared to baselines like DORN and Singh et al., while simultaneously achieving lower MAE and RMSE values.
*   We observed that TacoDepth (Plug-in) processes frames in 29.3ms, drastically faster than the comparable RadarCam-Depth at 358.3ms, while also achieving better accuracy.

**Intermediate Representation Analysis (from Figure 2):**
*   We analyzed intermediate "quasi-dense" depth maps produced by multi-stage methods.
*   Observation: These maps remained highly sparse with very few valid pixels (gray areas).
*   Observation: In adverse conditions (e.g., night scenes), the intermediate prediction failed almost completely, predicting no valid depth pixels in the regions of interest.

**Visual Depth Reconstruction (from Figure 4 - nuScenes):**
*   We compared visual outputs of Independent models in both daytime and nighttime scenarios.
*   Observation: Prior methods (RC-PDA, Singh et al.) exhibited disrupted geometric structures and noticeable artifacts.
*   Observation: TacoDepth produced depth maps with complete structures (e.g., clearly defined cars and buses) and finer details (e.g., pedestrian overpasses and metal guardrails).
*   Observation: In nighttime scenes, TacoDepth maintained robustness where other methods failed to resolve shapes.

**Plug-in Mode Visual Comparison (from Figure 5 - ZJU-4DRadarCam):**
*   We compared TacoDepth against RadarCam-Depth using the same initial depth predictor (DPT-Hybrid).
*   Observation: TacoDepth resolved complex structures (e.g., fences, distant walls) more clearly than RadarCam-Depth, which showed blurring in the highlighted regions.

**Ablation and Architecture Analysis (from Textual Analysis):**
*   We found that the Pyramid-based Radar fusion (PF) alone reduced MAE and RMSE by 12.4% and 8.7% respectively compared to the Singh et al. baseline using a simple MLP.
*   We found that replacing the MLP with the Graph-based Radar structure extractor (GE) further decreased MAE and RMSE by 5.7% and 5.5%.
*   We observed that increasing the layer count $L$ from 1 to 3 improved accuracy, but increasing to $L=4$ did not yield further improvements and decreased efficiency.
*   We achieved real-time processing speeds of over 37 fps with the independent model.
*   We reduced model parameters and FLOPs by 40.9% and 72.2% compared to Singh et al. (Independent mode).
*   We reduced model parameters and FLOPs by 57.1% and 77.4% compared to RadarCam-Depth (Plug-in mode).

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Radar-Camera depth estimation is critical for 3D perception in autonomous systems, yet current methodologies face significant efficiency and robustness bottlenecks. The primary obstacle stems from the intrinsic sparsity and noise of mmWave Radar data compared to LiDAR. To mitigate this, prevailing approaches utilize complex, multi-stage frameworks that generate intermediate "quasi-dense" depth maps to bridge the gap between sparse Radar returns and dense depth predictions.

This multi-stage paradigm is fundamentally flawed for two reasons. First, it is computationally inefficient, relying on serial processing steps that preclude real-time operation on resource-constrained vehicular hardware. Second, the intermediate quasi-dense depth remains sparse and prone to noise—particularly in adverse lighting or weather—leading to disrupted structures and artifacts in the final output. There is a critical need for a streamlined architecture that can directly regress dense metric depth from raw sparse Radar and image data without relying on defective intermediate representations.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can eliminate the intermediate quasi-dense depth stage entirely by redesigning how Radar information is extracted and fused. We propose "TacoDepth," a one-stage framework.

Our core technical hypothesis rests on two pillars:
1.  **Graph-Based Extraction:** Instead of treating Radar points as isolated coordinates (which is sensitive to outliers), we can capture robust geometric structures and topologies by modeling the Radar point cloud as a graph.
2.  **Pyramid-Based Fusion with Radar-Centered Attention:** We can achieve efficient, high-fidelity fusion by restricting cross-modal attention to valid horizontal proximity zones. Since 3D Radar elevation is noisy but horizontal azimuth is precise, a "Radar-centered" flash attention mechanism will allow us to correlate image pixels and Radar points efficiently, ignoring irrelevant background noise.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a one-stage architecture that takes a single RGB image $I \in \mathcal { R } ^ { H \times W \times 3 }$ and a Radar point cloud $P \in \mathcal { R } ^ { K \times 3 }$ (containing $K$ points) to predict a dense metric depth map $D \in \mathcal { R } ^ { H \times W }$.

### 1. Graph-based Radar Structure Extractor
To capture the geometric relations between sparse points, we will design a lightweight Graph Neural Network (GNN).
*   **Nodes & Edges:** Radar points $p \in \mathcal{R}^3$ serve as graph nodes. The adjacency matrix of these points constitutes the graph edges.
*   **Feature Update:** We will employ a PCA-GM based architecture to update and aggregate node features along edges.
*   **Hierarchical Output:** The extractor will contain $L=3$ layers. At each layer $l \in \{ 1 , 2 , 3 \}$, the module will output:
    *   Node features $N _ { l }$.
    *   Edge features $E _ { l }$.

### 2. Image Encoder and Pyramid-based Radar Fusion
We will utilize a ResNet-18 backbone as the image encoder to extract multi-scale feature maps $\{ F _ { 1 } , F _ { 2 } , \cdots , F _ { 2 L } \}$. The fusion module will integrate Radar and Image features in a pyramidal, hierarchical manner:
*   Node features $N _ { l }$ will be fused with image features $F _ { 2 l - 1 }$.
*   Edge features $E _ { l }$ will be fused with image features $F _ { 2 l }$.

### 3. Radar-Centered Flash Attention
To resolve the noise in Radar elevation and the computational cost of global attention, we will implement a masked attention mechanism based on horizontal coordinates.

**Defining the Attention Window:**
For a Radar point $p$ with horizontal coordinate $x_p$ and an image pixel $m$ with horizontal coordinate $x_m$, we define a validity window $a_l$. We will set the window widths for the three layers as $a_l \in \{ 48, 32, 16 \}$.

**Feature Sub-selection:**
We restrict the image feature map $F_{2l}$ to pixels falling within the horizontal window of the Radar points.
$$ \hat { F } _ { 2 l } = F _ { 2 l } \left[ x _ { p } - a _ { l } < x _ { m } < x _ { p } + a _ { l } \right] , \quad \hat { F } _ { 2 l } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { \hat { M } \times C _ { l } } $$
Where $\hat{M}$ is the reduced number of pixels and $C_l$ is the channel dimension. Similarly, for the edge features used as keys/values, we retain only points spatially adjacent to the query pixel:
$$ \hat { E } _ { l } = E _ { l } \left[ x _ { m } - a _ { l } < x _ { p } < x _ { m } + a _ { l } \right] , \quad \hat { E } _ { l } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { \hat { K } \times K } $$

**Attention Calculation:**
We compute the cross-modal correlation using a lightweight flash attention mechanism. For a pixel $m$, the query is derived from $\hat { F } _ { 2 l } [ m ]$, and keys/values are derived from $\hat { E } _ { l }$. Let $W_q, W_k, W_v$ be learnable linear projections. The fused feature $F'_{2l}$ is calculated as:
$$ F _ { 2 l } ^ { \prime } [ m ] = \mathrm { s o f t m a x } \left( \frac { W _ { q } \hat { F } _ { 2 l } [ m ] \left( W _ { k } \hat { E } _ { l } \right) ^ { T } } { \sqrt { C _ { l } } } \right) W _ { v } \hat { E } _ { l } $$
This process is wrapped in attention blocks with MLPs and residual connections. The resulting fused features $\{ F _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \cdots , F _ { 2 L } ^ { \prime } \}$ are passed to a depth decoder to predict the final metric depth $D$.

### 4. Flexible Inference Mode (Dual-Branch)
To allow the model to operate either independently or as a plug-in for existing relative depth estimators, we will introduce an auxiliary input branch.
*   **Formulation:** $D = { \mathcal { T } } _ { \theta } { \big ( } I , P \mid D ^ { * } { \big ) }$, where $D^*$ is an optional initial relative depth map.
*   **Mechanism:** If $D^*$ is provided, the auxiliary branch processes it and fuses it with image features. If not (independent mode), the branch input is zeroed.

### 5. Loss Formulation
We will train the model using supervised learning with LiDAR ground truth ($D_{gt}$) and accumulated semi-dense depth from temporal reprojection ($D_{acc}$). The loss function will be an $L_1$ loss:
$$ \ell _ { L _ { 1 } } = \frac { 1 } { \left| \Omega _ { g t } \right| } \sum _ { \Omega _ { g t } } \left| D - D _ { g t } \right| + \frac { \lambda } { \left| \Omega _ { a c c } \right| } \sum _ { \Omega _ { a c c } } \left| D - D _ { a c c } \right| $$
Here, $\Omega_{gt}$ and $\Omega_{acc}$ are the validity masks for the respective ground truth sources, and we will set the weighting coefficient $\lambda = 1$.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Efficiency:** By replacing multi-stage depth completion pipelines with a one-stage GNN-based fusion, we expect to significantly reduce inference latency and FLOPs.
2.  **Structural Robustness:** The proposed graph-based extractor will allow the network to learn topological consistency in the point cloud, making the depth estimation robust to the sparsity and jitter typical of automotive Radar sensors.
3.  **Architectural Unification:** The auxiliary branch design unifies the "independent" and "plug-in" paradigms, allowing a single architecture to function as a standalone estimator or a metric-scale refiner for state-of-the-art relative depth models.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
